article.title: Why “Done” Should Have a Clear Meaning
article.why: Workplace English for defining completion criteria and reducing rework.
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
A team can lose time when different people use the word “done” in different ways. One person may think a task is done when the first draft exists. Another may think it is done only after review. A third person may expect testing, approval, and documentation too. If the meaning is unclear, work can look finished even when important steps are still missing.

A simple Definition of Done can solve this problem. It is a short list of conditions that must be true before the team calls a piece of work complete. For example, a small data report might be done only when the numbers have been checked, the file has been shared, and the owner has confirmed that no correction is needed.

The definition should match the type of work. A software change may need code review and testing. A client slide may need updated numbers and manager approval. A monthly report may need a source check and a final version saved in the correct folder. The goal is not to create many rules. The goal is to remove hidden expectations.

A clear meaning of “done” also makes status updates easier. Instead of saying, “I think this is almost done,” a team member can say, “The analysis is complete, but the review is still open.” This makes the remaining work visible.

The definition can change when the team learns something. If a repeated mistake appears, the team may add one new check. If a step no longer adds value, the team may remove it. The definition is useful only when people actually use it.

Before starting repeated work, ask one question: What must be true before we can safely call this done? A short answer can prevent many rounds of rework.

This is especially helpful when work moves between people. The next person does not need to guess whether “done” means drafted, reviewed, or delivered. Everyone can check the same conditions. A shared standard makes handovers clearer and helps the team notice unfinished work before it becomes someone else’s problem.

grammar.title: Contrast and qualification
grammar.body: Use structures such as “does not automatically mean” and “rather than” to separate related but different ideas.

business.term: What must be true before we call this done?
business.example: Before we start, what must be true before we call this done?
